In this video, I take four 12V batteries and wire them in series to create a 48V battery bank. But the real focus is the part a lot of people skip: keeping those batteries balanced.

When you build a 24V, 36V, or 48V battery system using multiple 12V batteries in series, each battery can slowly drift to a different state of charge. One battery may end up higher, another lower, and the lowest battery can limit the performance of the whole system.

In some cases, the weakest or lowest battery becomes the one that shuts everything down early.

That is why a battery balancer matters.

🔋 WHAT YOU’LL LEARN

- How 4× 12V batteries make a 48V battery bank
- Why batteries in series can get out of balance
- How a 12V battery balancer works in a 48V system
- How to connect balancing leads
- LiTime battery balancer installation overview
- ECO-Worthy battery balancer installation overview
- Lead-acid vs. LiFePO4 balancing considerations
- Why balancing can help usable capacity
- Why balancing may help long-term battery health
- Why a 4×12V battery bank is different from a true 16-cell 48V battery pack with one BMS

⚡ WHY SERIES BATTERIES DRIFT

When batteries are wired in series, the voltage adds together, but each 12V battery is still its own battery with its own BMS, cells, limits, and state of charge.

Over time, small differences can add up.

That can happen because of:

- Slightly different internal resistance
- Different battery age or condition
- BMS cutoff differences
- Charging differences
- Load differences
- Cell balancing differences inside each battery
- Not fully charging or balancing the bank

A balancer helps move energy between batteries so one battery does not get too far ahead or behind the others.

🔧 WHY THIS MATTERS FOR 48V DIY SOLAR

A 48V battery bank built from four 12V batteries can work, but it needs to be treated correctly.

This type of setup is common in:

- RV solar systems
- Off-grid sheds
- Backup power systems
- Inverter builds
- DIY solar projects
- Mobile power systems

But if the batteries drift too far apart, your inverter may shut down early even though the battery bank appears to have capacity left.

Balancing helps the bank act more like one system instead of four separate batteries fighting each other.

snippet.description:

What better time to test emergency backup power than during a real Florida thunderstorm?

In this video, I put the Efurden 4400W inverter generator to work and show how I use an EG4 Chargeverter to recharge an off-grid battery system when solar production drops during storms, hurricanes, extended cloudy weather, and grid outages.

This is a real-world disaster preparedness test, not a lab test. I look at generator performance, charging behavior, practical backup strategy, and why a generator can be one of the most useful tools in a solar backup system.

⚡ WHAT THIS SETUP DOES

* Uses the Efurden inverter generator as a portable AC power source
* Uses the EG4 Chargeverter to turn generator power into battery charging
* Helps recharge an off-grid battery bank when solar is limited
* Gives you a way to run the generator for charging instead of relying on it all night
* Adds flexibility for hurricanes, storms, outages, and emergency backup

🔋 WHY A GENERATOR + CHARGEVERTER MAKES SENSE

Solar is great when the sun is out. But during storms, hurricanes, long cloudy stretches, or heavy emergency use, solar production may not keep up.

A generator can fill that gap.

Instead of using a generator to run every load continuously, you can use it to recharge your battery bank. Then your inverter can run the refrigerator, lights, internet, fans, CPAP, or other critical loads from battery power.

That can mean less generator runtime, less noise, less fuel use, and a more flexible backup plan.

⚠️ IMPORTANT BACKUP POWER NOTE

A generator, Chargeverter, battery bank, and inverter all need to be sized correctly for the loads and charging current you plan to use. Always verify generator output, input voltage, wire size, breaker ratings, grounding, ventilation, fuel safety, battery limits, and manufacturer instructions before connecting any emergency power system.
